MIRIX-2.0: Multi-Agent Memory System

Wei-Chieh Huang Affiliation: MIRIX AI Equal contribution    Weizhi Zhang Affiliation: MIRIX AI Equal contribution Corresponding author    Jiayan Nan Affiliation: MIRIX AI Equal contribution    Peng Xia Affiliation: MIRIX AI Equal contribution    Yu Wang Affiliation: MIRIX AI Equal contribution Corresponding author
Abstract

Long-term memory lets LLM agents personalize, stay consistent, and reuse what worked before. Parametric memories need training, consolidation can lose details for good, and keeping every record leaves a growing store to search. We present MIRIX-2.0, a multi-agent memory system designed to be practical, accurate, and efficient at once. It is the most accurate of the compared systems on four of five QA benchmarks. It reaches 91.4% on LoCoMo and 72.6% on LongMemEval-S, where it leads the strongest baseline by 14.3 points, and with AutoDream disabled it gains 31.0 and 22.0 points over HyperMem on single-hop and multi-hop document QA. As procedural memory, it yields the highest mean success among the compared memory methods on ALFWorld and WebShop and reaches 49.2% on MetaClaw-Bench, against 44.0% for MetaClaw’s skill library. Six typed memory agents keep complete records as the system of record, and a provenance hypergraph indexes episodic and semantic records with n-ary frames that cite their rows. Retrieval runs under explicit budgets, so the evidence a question inspects does not grow with the history. AutoDream merges duplicate anchors outside the write path without rewriting any record, and it distills task sessions into skills. With AutoDream disabled, MIRIX-2.0 answers faster than HyperMem on all five timed benchmarks. It needs no fine-tuning, runs with closed and open models, and its code is public.

††Website: https://mirix.io/††GitHub: https://github.com/Mirix-AI/MIRIX

1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents now work over horizons far longer than a single context window (Luo et al., 2025b; Huang et al., 2026b). A personal agent accumulates months of conversation with its user, and a task agent meets similar problems across many episodes. Memory lets such agents carry information across sessions (Wang et al., 2025a), so that they can personalize their responses (Zhang et al., 2026e), stay consistent with what they were told (Packer et al., 2023; Chhikara et al., 2025), and reuse what worked before (Wang et al., 2025e; Xia et al., 2026a). Benchmarks now measure this ability on long conversations (Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025), long documents (Hu et al., 2026), multi-session agentic tasks (He et al., 2026), and lifelong personalization (Zhang et al., 2026d).

Benchmarks score a memory by its answers, but a team that deploys one asks more of it. A memory that agents can rely on in practice has to meet three requirements at once. It has to be accurate about the particulars of past experience, such as a name, a date, a count, or the distinction between two events, and about the connections between them. It has to be practical, which means deployable with the models a team already uses, nothing to train, answers that can be traced to stored records, and consolidation that cannot destroy what was stored. It also has to be efficient, with answer latency and token cost per question that stay bounded as the history grows.

Each family of existing systems gives up at least one of the three. Systems that consolidate records into extracted facts or abstractions (Chhikara et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026) are compact but give up accuracy: the details they discard are gone for good, and consolidation can make a memory faulty even when it is distilled from useful experience (Zhang et al., 2026a). Systems that keep every record and retrieve from them directly lose nothing but give up efficiency, since retrieval must search an ever larger and noisier history (Huang et al., 2026b). Graph memories organize the same content around entities and their relations (Rasmussen et al., 2025; Edge et al., 2024), but binary triples split an n-ary fact into fragments and lose the connections among its participants (Luo et al., 2025a). Hypergraph memories (Yue et al., 2026) group episodes under topics and facts under episodes, but their hyperedges record which unit belongs where rather than the participants of a fact, and retrieval descends from topic summaries written at storage time, so a detail is reachable only after its topic has been retrieved. File-system memories, such as the auto memory of Claude Code (Anthropic, 2026), route retrieval through summaries in the same way: they keep notes in plain files behind a size-capped index that is loaded into every session, and the agent opens a file on the strength of its one-line summary. A detail that no summary mentions is reachable only by string search, which neither resolves an entity across files nor follows its relations, and index entries past the cap are not loaded at the start of a session. Both families prune top down to bound their cost, and both pay for the pruning with recall on details their summaries do not reflect. Parametric memories store experience in model weights or latent states (Wang et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025c; Behrouz et al., 2025) and give up practicality, since they require training and rule out closed models.

The requirements also weigh differently for the two uses of memory. Recent studies separate user-centric memory, which personalizes an agent to its user, from agent-centric memory, which accumulates the agent’s own experience, and they find that the two face reversed challenges (Huang et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2026c). A user-centric memory has to record a user’s history broadly and connect its pieces, because a later question may depend on any detail of that history (Zhang et al., 2026d; Ma et al., 2026b). An agent-centric memory has to be precise and refined instead. It distills trajectories into strategies and skills (Zhao et al., 2024; Ouyang et al., 2026; Xia et al., 2026b), and retrieving too much can pull the agent’s attention away from the context that matters for its next action (Huang et al., 2026c). A practical system has to serve both uses from one store. Figures 2 and 3 trace one example of each setting through MIRIX-2.0.

In this work, we present MIRIX-2.0, a multi-agent memory system designed to be practical, accurate, and efficient at once. It keeps the multi-agent design of MIRIX (Wang and Chen, 2025) and rethinks how memory is stored, indexed, retrieved, and consolidated so that a specific layer meets each requirement (Figure 1). Six memory agents under a Meta Memory Manager write complete records to a typed evidence plane in a vector database, the system of record, so details survive consolidation and every graph fact the answer receives cites the rows it came from. The graph is only an index. The database write commits first, a failed graph write never rolls back a stored memory, and a failed graph read falls back to direct evidence retrieval. A provenance hypergraph indexes the entities, events, relations, roles, and times in episodic and semantic records as n-ary frames that cite the rows they were extracted from and carry dates, prices, and counts as literals, and undated events with similar wording keep distinct identities. At query time, a deterministic planner sets explicit budgets, retrieval enters the hypergraph at the anchors that match the question, and the answer receives graph facts together with the records they cite (Section 2.4). The evidence a question inspects is therefore bounded by construction and does not grow with the length of the history.

Like sleep-time and offline consolidation methods (Lin et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026), AutoDream consolidates memory outside the write path, and it treats the two kinds of memory in opposite ways. For semantic memory, it consolidates identities and never rewrites evidence. It pairs each anchor introduced by new semantic rows with its nearest anchors of the same identity-stable type, such as a person or a place, and asks a language model whether a pair denotes one entity. A confirmed merge unites the citations of the two anchors and rewires the frames that mention them, while event anchors, fact frames, and stored records stay unchanged, so a merge can never destroy a stored memory. Its cost depends on the newly written semantic frontier rather than on the total size of memory, verification runs under explicit pair caps, and negative decisions are cached so that later cycles do not pay for the same pair again. For procedural memory, AutoDream refines instead. It judges each finished task session from quotes in its transcript, distills lessons worth reusing and mistakes worth avoiding, and lets a curator (Zhang et al., 2026c) create or edit skills whose edits can cite the experiences behind them.

We evaluate MIRIX-2.0 on conversational memory, long-document question answering, personalized generation, and procedural memory for interactive agents. MIRIX-2.0 has the highest accuracy of all compared memory systems on both conversational benchmarks, 91.4% on LoCoMo in our runs and 72.6% on LongMemEval-S, 14.3 points above the strongest baseline. On LoCoMo, the hypergraph raises accuracy over flat memory from 85.7% to 88.4%, with the largest gain on multi-hop questions, and AutoDream raises every question type and lifts the overall score to 91.4%. On LongMemEval-S, the hypergraph alone adds 11.2 points. On the single-hop and multi-hop document QA tasks of MemoryAgentBench (Hu et al., 2026), with AutoDream disabled, it answers 83.0% and 71.0% of the questions, 31.0 and 22.0 points above the strongest baseline, and on MemoryCD (Zhang et al., 2026d) it has the highest value on all four metrics for cross-domain review summarization. Used as procedural memory, MIRIX-2.0 gives the highest mean success among the compared memory methods on ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021), at 76.4% with GPT-6 Luna against 73.6% for Agent Workflow Memory (AWM) (Wang et al., 2025e) and 69.4% without memory, and on WebShop (Yao et al., 2022), at 37.4%. With GPT-5.2 it reaches 49.2% accuracy on MetaClaw-Bench (Xia et al., 2026b), against 44.0% reported for the MetaClaw skill library.

What makes these results usable is the cost at which they come. With AutoDream disabled, MIRIX-2.0 answers faster than HyperMem, the strongest baseline, on all five benchmarks we timed, ingests the two conversational benchmarks in less time, and uses fewer answer tokens on four of the five. As procedural memory, on WebShop it uses the fewest training and test tokens among the memory methods while reaching the highest success. The cost is paid when long documents are ingested. Building the graph makes their ingestion about four times slower than flat memory and slower than that baseline. The full system with AutoDream is not timed, and the retrieval bounds cover the evidence a question inspects, not latency measured as the history grows. No model is fine-tuned, the same system runs with closed and open models, and the code is public.

Our contributions are as follows.

  • •

    Accurate and practical. A layered memory design in which six typed memory agents keep complete records as the system of record and a provenance-preserving n-ary hypergraph serves only as their index, with occurrence identities that keep distinct events apart and fail-soft indexing that never rolls back a stored memory.

  • •

    One memory for users and agents. To the best of our knowledge, MIRIX-2.0 is the first memory system that handles both user-centric and agent-centric memory, serving personalization and the refinement of agent skills from one store.

  • •

    Efficient and safe to consolidate. Graph-owned retrieval runs under explicit budgets and returns graph facts together with the records that justify them. AutoDream merges duplicate entity anchors under explicit caps without touching stored memories, which adds 3.0 points on LoCoMo, and distills task sessions into skills for procedural memory.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents MIRIX-2.0. It states the problem and the three technical requirements, introduces the typed evidence plane and the provenance hypergraph that indexes it, describes graph-owned retrieval under explicit budgets, and explains how AutoDream consolidates semantic and procedural memory outside the write path. Section 3 evaluates the accuracy of MIRIX-2.0 on conversational recall, long-document question answering, and personalized generation, its use as agent memory on ALFWorld, WebShop, and MetaClaw-Bench, and its cost in ingestion time, answer latency, and tokens. Section 4 relates MIRIX-2.0 to prior work on memory systems for LLM agents, multi-agent systems, and memory consolidation, and Section 5 concludes and discusses the limitations of this study. Appendix A gives the details of the method, and Appendix B gives the full results behind the figures.

2 Methodology

MIRIX-2.0 is designed to be practical, accurate, and efficient. It has to run with the models a team already uses and leave stored records intact, it has to keep a name, a date, a count, or the distinction between two events recoverable after writing and after consolidation, and it has to answer from a bounded evidence set however long the history grows. This section describes the layered design that delivers the three.

MIRIX-2.0 separates storage from indexing (Figure 1). A typed evidence plane stores complete memories and is the system of record (Section 2.2). A provenance hypergraph indexes the entities, events, relations, roles, and times in those memories, and every fact in it cites the records it came from (Section 2.3). Three paths operate on the two layers, and Algorithm 1 states each of them in pseudocode. The write path stores a memory and then indexes it. The read path plans a query, traverses the graph, and dereferences only the records it selects (Section 2.4). AutoDream, the third path, runs outside the other two (Section 2.5). On semantic memory it merges duplicate anchors in the hypergraph and returns the evidence store unchanged, so semantic consolidation changes how evidence is connected, never what evidence exists. On procedural memory, AutoDream instead distills task sessions into skills that cite the experiences behind them. Section A.6 collects the properties that hold regardless of how the language models behave.

2.1 Problem setup

For a user uu, the system observes a stream 𝒳u=(x1,…,xT)\mathcal{X}_{u}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T}) of conversational or multimodal inputs. When it writes xtx_{t}, future queries are unknown, so the writer must produce a persistent state

𝒮ut=(Put,Gut)\mathcal{S}_{u}^{t}=(P_{u}^{t},G_{u}^{t}) (1)

from which a later query qq can be answered with a bounded evidence set ℛ⁡(q,𝒮ut)\mathcal{R}(q;\mathcal{S}_{u}^{t}). The evidence store PuP_{u} collects the typed stores, among them the episodic store PuEP_{u}^{E}, the semantic store PuSP_{u}^{S}, and the procedural store PuPP_{u}^{P}. We seek high answer utility under three technical requirements.

  1. 1.

    Source fidelity. Concrete evidence remains recoverable after writing and after consolidation.

  2. 2.

    Bounded access. A query inspects a small graph neighborhood and a bounded set of cited rows instead of scanning the full history.

  3. 3.

    Temporal identity. Repeated descriptions of one event may share evidence, but distinct occurrences must not collapse merely because they are worded alike.

Source fidelity and temporal identity are what make the system accurate and its answers traceable, and bounded access is what keeps it efficient. The rest of this section shows how the two layers meet these requirements. Each subsection explains a block of Algorithm 1, and the numbers on its right point to the equations that define each step.

2.2 Typed evidence plane

Multi-agent routing.

A Meta Memory Manager routes each input xtx_{t} to the subset 𝒦t=Rθ​(xt)\mathcal{K}_{t}=R_{\theta}(x_{t}) of memory types it updates (Algorithm 1, line 2). Each of the six types, Core, Episodic, Semantic, Procedural, Resource, and Knowledge Vault, has its own writer, and the writer of a selected type kk produces the record mt(k)=Wk​(xt,Put−1)m_{t}^{(k)}=W_{k}(x_{t},P_{u}^{t-1}) and owns the schema and update operations of that type. Only episodic and semantic records are indexed by the hypergraph. Section A.1 gives the roles of the six types and the reason for this split.

Evidence records.

Each of the six memory types keeps its records in its own schema. The hypergraph indexes the episodic and semantic records, and each of them is represented as

m=(i,k,y,τe,τm,ρ,𝐳),m=(i,k,y,\tau_{e},\tau_{m},\rho,\mathbf{z}), (2)

where ii is an immutable row identifier, k∈{episodic,semantic}k\in\{\mathrm{episodic},\mathrm{semantic}\} is its memory type, yy is the stored text, τe\tau_{e} is the event time when one applies, τm\tau_{m} is the mention or write time, ρ\rho records source and chunk provenance, and 𝐳\mathbf{z} holds the search embeddings. Full summaries and details remain in the vector database. The graph stores only identifiers and compact structural metadata.

Writers keep concrete details such as names, counts, and dates in each record, and a record is committed to the vector database before graph construction begins (line 3), so a failed graph write never rolls back a stored memory (Section A.1).

2.3 A provenance-preserving n-ary hypergraph

The second half of the write path turns each episodic or semantic record into graph structure (Algorithm 1, lines 5–9). For each user, MIRIX-2.0 maintains a hypergraph

Gu=(𝒜u,ℱu,ℰu)G_{u}=(\mathcal{A}_{u},\mathcal{F}_{u},\mathcal{E}_{u}) (3)

with entity or concept anchors 𝒜u\mathcal{A}_{u}, reified fact frames ℱu\mathcal{F}_{u}, and role-typed incidence edges ℰu\mathcal{E}_{u}. Section A.7 shows the hypergraph MIRIX-2.0 builds for one LoCoMo conversation.

Anchors.

An anchor

a=(ia,na,ta,𝐞a,IaE,IaS)a=(i_{a},n_{a},t_{a},\mathbf{e}_{a},I_{a}^{E},I_{a}^{S}) (4)

stores a canonical name nan_{a}, an entity type tat_{a}, a name embedding 𝐞a\mathbf{e}_{a}, and the identifiers IaEI_{a}^{E} and IaSI_{a}^{S} of the episodic and semantic rows that mention it. A deterministic key κ⁡(n)\kappa(n) normalizes case, punctuation, function words, word order, and singular and plural variants of a name while keeping numbers, and a deterministic admission gate rejects generic filing terms and dialogue-role pseudo-entities and caps the anchors admitted from one record (Section A.2).

Registry-guided canonicalization.

Surface normalization cannot decide whether two semantically close names denote the same entity. For every extracted entity, approximate nearest-neighbor search therefore retrieves a few existing anchors of the user above a similarity threshold, and one language-model call per record makes a conservative same-entity decision for all of its entities. A rename is accepted only when it selects a retrieved candidate, so embeddings propose comparisons but never authorize a merge on their own. The neighbor count and the threshold, with their relation to the vector-index score, are in Section A.2.

N-ary frames.

For each episodic or semantic record, an extractor produces a set of frames

f=(p,{(rj,aj)}j=1df,ℓf,τe,τm,Cf),f=\left(p,\,\{(r_{j},a_{j})\}_{j=1}^{d_{f}},\,\ell_{f},\,\tau_{e},\tau_{m},\,C_{f}\right), (5)

where pp is a canonical predicate, rjr_{j} is the open-vocabulary role of anchor aja_{j}, ℓf\ell_{f} maps literal attributes to their values, and CfC_{f} is the set of identifiers of the vector-database records the frame cites. A flight, for example, becomes one frame with agent, origin, destination, carrier, and companion arms instead of several disconnected triples, and owns(Mia, Suica card) in Figure 2 is a frame that cites the May 2 record. The extractor is instructed to keep dates, prices, counts, durations, and measurements as literals on the frame rather than as anchors, so that a value stays attached to the assertion it qualifies. A frame is materialized only if its arguments resolve to at least two distinct anchors of the user. When a deterministic audit finds that the extraction misses high-signal source details, one bounded repair call may add frames that the source supports, and it cannot remove anything the primary extraction produced. Section A.2 describes the audit.

Occurrence identity.

Semantic claims and episodic occurrences follow different identity rules. Let σ⁡(f)\sigma(f) be the sorted set of role and anchor keys {rj:κ⁡(naj)}\{r_{j}:\kappa(n_{a_{j}})\}. A semantic frame is identified by

idS⁡(f)=H⁡(u,p,σ⁡(f)),\operatorname{id}_{S}(f)=H(u,p,\sigma(f)), (6)

so repeated support for the same durable claim accumulates citations on one node. An episodic frame adds an occurrence key,

idE⁡(f)\displaystyle\operatorname{id}_{E}(f) =H⁡(u,p,σ⁡(f),χ⁡(f)),\displaystyle=H(u,p,\sigma(f),\chi(f)), (7)
χ⁡(f)\displaystyle\chi(f) ={explicit event time,if extracted,immutable memory id,otherwise.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\text{explicit event time},&\text{if extracted},\\ \text{immutable memory id},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (8)

Two mentions of the same dated event therefore share one frame, while two undated events with similar wording, such as two runs on different days, stay separate. A frame keeps the time of the event apart from the time it was mentioned, and whether the event is planned or done does not change its identity.

2.4 Graph-owned evidence retrieval

MIRIX-2.0 treats retrieval as the construction of a bounded evidence set rather than as open-ended similarity search. Episodic and semantic candidates must enter through the graph, and the vector database dereferences and reranks only the identifiers that graph traversal selects. This boundary keeps a hidden full-table search from doing the work attributed to the graph. Only a graph read that raises an error falls back to direct evidence retrieval. A query passes through planning, anchor entry, expansion along two evidence lanes, and fusion, and a verifier then checks the answer (Algorithm 1, lines 12–19). For the question in Figure 2, the planner chooses the single operator, enters the graph at Mia and Tokyo transit, and returns three facts with five rows.

Query plan.

A deterministic planner maps a query to

Π⁡(q)=(oq,𝒫q,𝒞q,𝒴q,𝒯q,BqB,BqR),\Pi(q)=\left(o_{q},\mathcal{P}_{q},\mathcal{C}_{q},\mathcal{Y}_{q},\mathcal{T}_{q},B_{q}^{B},B_{q}^{R}\right), (9)

where the operator oqo_{q} is single, temporal, intersection, list-union, or count, 𝒫q\mathcal{P}_{q} holds canonical relation families and their surface forms, 𝒞q\mathcal{C}_{q} holds non-relational constraints, 𝒴q\mathcal{Y}_{q} holds expected answer types, and 𝒯q\mathcal{T}_{q} holds date and temporal-order constraints. The two budgets cap the base-recall rows and the relation-cited rows, and BqRB_{q}^{R} also caps the graph facts that the relation lane renders. The budgets grow with the operator, from 6 base rows and 4 cited rows for a single-value lookup to 8 and 12 for a count, since counting and set construction need broader evidence. Table 6 in Section A.3 lists all five operators.

Anchor entry.

The query embedding first recalls fifteen anchors by name. A relation query adds the anchors that the question names exactly, and the union is scored by

sA​(a,q)=svec+sexact+slex+spred+sspec−shub.s_{A}(a,q)=s_{\mathrm{vec}}+s_{\mathrm{exact}}+s_{\mathrm{lex}}+s_{\mathrm{pred}}+s_{\mathrm{spec}}-s_{\mathrm{hub}}. (10)

The vector score dominates. Exact mention, token overlap, predicate compatibility, and multi-token specificity break close ties, and a logarithmic degree penalty suppresses generic hubs. The top fifteen anchors are kept, which is the cap KAK_{A} of Algorithm 1. The cap on exactly named anchors and the hub and predicate rules are in Section A.3.

Two evidence lanes.

The selected anchors open two bounded lanes. In the base-recall lane, anchors yield the episodic and semantic identifiers directly associated with them, and traversing an incident n-ary frame adds the frame’s cited memories and a bounded set of memories associated with its co-participants. In the relation-citation lane, which opens when the query plan contains a relation, the exactly named anchors seed an indexed adjacency lookup over their incident frames. Predicate filtering applies before a cap of 240 frames, the fact score below ranks the rest, and at most BqRB_{q}^{R} of them are rendered as explicit graph facts that contribute their exact citations into the vector database. The provenance recomputation of the base lane and the object filter of the relation lane are in Section A.3.

Fact scoring.

Each relation-lane frame receives the additive score

sF​(f,q)=\displaystyle s_{F}(f,q)={} srel+sentity+sconstraint+stype\displaystyle s_{\mathrm{rel}}+s_{\mathrm{entity}}+s_{\mathrm{constraint}}+s_{\mathrm{type}}
+stime+sintersection+sspecificity\displaystyle+s_{\mathrm{time}}+s_{\mathrm{intersection}}+s_{\mathrm{specificity}}
+srole+sstate.\displaystyle+s_{\mathrm{role}}+s_{\mathrm{state}}. (11)

The first seven terms score relation, named-entity, literal, answer-type, and temporal compatibility, a shared object for intersection questions, and the number of arguments a frame binds. The role term sroles_{\mathrm{role}} rewards agreement between the argument direction implied by the question and the frame’s typed roles, and it penalizes incompatible roles. The state term sstates_{\mathrm{state}} rewards an event time that matches a requested date and penalizes planned occurrences in count, list-union, and temporal questions. Section A.3 describes its fallback and the treatment of intersection questions.

Citation-balanced fusion.

Rows in each lane are reranked, and fusion takes up to BqRB_{q}^{R} cited rows, then up to BqBB_{q}^{B} base rows, and fills the remaining capacity from the rest of either lane without duplicating row identifiers. The returned evidence therefore contains both the graph facts and the source rows that justify them. The reranking prior, the per-type split, and the rule for near-duplicate paraphrases are also in Section A.3.

Answer-time verification.

In our harness, the answering agent may call the retriever up to five times. After it drafts an answer, a rule-based check requests one more search and one rewrite by the answering model when the draft shows explicit uncertainty, lacks a value the question asks for, or disagrees with the evidence ledger, for example a count without a number or a month that neither the evidence nor the question contains. It also fires on every intersection question (line 19). The check runs in the answering agent rather than in the memory server, and it never inspects a reference answer. Section A.4 lists every trigger and the query of the extra search.

2.5 AutoDream: consolidation outside the write path

AutoDream runs outside the critical write path (Algorithm 1, lines 22–29). It treats the two kinds of memory it consolidates in opposite ways. On semantic memory it is an explicit service call that never schedules itself, and it refines identities under the contract

Dream⁡(Pu,Gu,Δu)=(Pu,G~u),\operatorname{Dream}(P_{u},G_{u};\Delta_{u})=(P_{u},\widetilde{G}_{u}), (12)

where Δu\Delta_{u} is the newly written semantic frontier and G~u\widetilde{G}_{u} is the consolidated hypergraph. The evidence store PuP_{u} is returned unchanged. On procedural memory it starts in the background once five task sessions are pending, and it turns them into skills.

Semantic frontier.

Each call receives the exact source-chunk identifiers of the batch just written, which resolve to the newly written semantic rows. These rows define a small frontier Δu\Delta_{u}, so the cost of consolidation depends on new activity rather than on the total size of memory. The invocation schedule of our protocol is in Section A.5.

Candidate generation.

Only anchors that are backed by semantic rows and belong to an identity-stable type t∈𝒯safe={person, organization, location, object, concept}t\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{safe}}=\{\text{person, organization, location, object, concept}\} are eligible. For each eligible anchor a∈𝒜Δa\in\mathcal{A}_{\Delta} backed by a frontier row, AutoDream takes the four nearest entries of the name index, which include aa itself, and forms the candidate pairs

𝒞Δ={(a,b):a∈𝒜Δ,b∈NN4(a)∖{a},cos⁡(𝐞a,𝐞b)≥0.86,ta=tb∈𝒯safe}.\mathcal{C}_{\Delta}=\left\{(a,b):\begin{array}[]{l}a\in\mathcal{A}_{\Delta},\;b\in\operatorname{NN}_{4}(a)\setminus\{a\},\\ \cos(\mathbf{e}_{a},\mathbf{e}_{b})\geq 0.86,\\ t_{a}=t_{b}\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{safe}}\end{array}\right\}. (13)

Episodic-only anchors are excluded by construction. An LLM decides whether each pair denotes the same entity and, if it does, chooses one of the two existing names as the canonical representative. Its output is constrained to the submitted pair, and invented representatives are rejected. In Figure 3, steel bottle and stainless steel bottle form such a pair.

Bounded schedule.

Every Dream round verifies at most a fixed number of unseen pairs, and the final round also considers the eligible anchors that no earlier round used as a source. Explicit negative decisions are cached as the set 𝒩\mathcal{N} of Algorithm 1, so later cycles do not pay again to reconsider the same pair. Section A.5 states the caps of the intermediate, final, and repair rounds and the cache key.

Lossless structural merge.

For a confirmed merge a→ba\rightarrow b, the system unions the episodic and semantic row identifiers, keeps aliases, sums mention counts, keeps the maximum admission score, and rewires every role-typed frame arm to bb. Union, sum, and maximum are commutative and associative, so the order of repeated merges does not change the reachable evidence. The dropped anchor is removed only after its values and edges have been transferred.

Semantic Dream never rewrites the memories in the vector database, and it consolidates neither episodic-only anchors nor fact nodes. The asymmetry is deliberate. Semantic identity can be refined incrementally, whereas event occurrences and their citations are kept as observations. AutoDream therefore makes the graph less fragmented without creating a textual summary whose embedding could hide the details of its inputs.

Procedural refinement.

For procedural memory, AutoDream refines instead of merging. A distiller judges the outcome of each pending session from quotes in its transcript and distills experiences e1,…,eme_{1},\ldots,e_{m}, each marked as a lesson worth reusing or a mistake worth avoiding. A curator (Zhang et al., 2026c) turns these experiences into skills in the procedural store PuPP_{u}^{P}, and it can create, edit, or delete a skill. An edit can cite the experiences behind it with a quote of the text it adds, and a citation is recorded only when that quote checks out, so a cited step of a skill can be traced through its experiences to the quoted sessions they came from. In Figure 3, one failed purchase yields an experience to avoid and one to reuse, and the curator adds two steps to the shopping routine that cite the first and keeps a step that the second supports. The distiller’s unclear verdict and the curator’s non-edit verdicts are in Section A.5. \FloatBarrier

3 Experiments

We evaluate MIRIX-2.0 for the three properties it is designed for. Accuracy is measured for user memory on conversational recall, document QA, and personalized generation (Section 3.2), which mainly exercise semantic memory together with the episodic records that ground it, and for agent memory on held-out interactive tasks and on MetaClaw-Bench, whose tasks span 30 days (Section 3.3), which exercise procedural memory. Efficiency is measured as ingestion time, answer latency, and answer tokens for user memory, with AutoDream disabled in every timed run, and as training and test tokens for agents (Section 3.4). Practicality is built into the protocol itself. One system serves both uses, no model is fine-tuned, the agent evaluation covers closed and open backbones, and every graph configuration runs under the budgets of Section 2.4.

3.1 Experimental setup and system variants

Default system and ablations.

Unless a configuration is explicitly identified otherwise, MIRIX-2.0 denotes the full architecture with the provenance hypergraph and AutoDream enabled. For the user-memory ablations, M0 uses flat vector memory without the graph or AutoDream, like MIRIX-1.0 (Wang and Chen, 2025), and the tables label it MIRIX-1.0. M1 adds graph indexing and retrieval but disables AutoDream, and M2 is the full graph plus AutoDream configuration. M1 and M2 are configurations of MIRIX-2.0, not successive releases of the method. In M2, semantic AutoDream is invoked by the ingestion driver after every five chunks and after the final chunk, outside the critical write path (Section 2.5 and Section A.5). It merges eligible entity anchors while preserving stored records and episodic occurrences.

The conversational tables report all three configurations. The available document QA results and graph efficiency measurements use M1 and are labeled accordingly; disabling AutoDream there is an experimental choice, not a restriction that prevents consolidation of document memories. MemoryCD is reported under the system name, but its recorded results do not identify an M0, M1, or M2 configuration, so we do not use them to estimate the contribution of AutoDream. For agent memory, we evaluate the procedural refinement path, in which AutoDream distills sessions into reusable skills whose retrieval is independent of the semantic hypergraph. The M0, M1, and M2 comparisons below therefore concern user-memory indexing and semantic consolidation, rather than a procedural graph ablation.

User-memory tasks and baselines.

LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024) and LongMemEval-S (Wu et al., 2025) test conversational recall. SHDocQA, MHDocQA, and DetectiveQA in the MemoryAgentBench evaluation (Hu et al., 2026) extend this analysis to factual and relational evidence in documents. They are evidence-retrieval tests rather than direct personalization tasks. MemoryCD (Zhang et al., 2026d) tests whether stored user information supports personalized review summarization and generation. We compare with mem0, A-Mem, MemoryBank, Graphiti, and HyperMem on QA, and with the methods listed in the MemoryCD tables, including long-context and RAG baselines, on personalization.

Models and scoring.

For the user-memory evaluation, the answerer and extractor use gpt-4.1-mini with temperature 0 and seed 42, and the topic extractor uses gpt-4.1-nano. MIRIX-2.0 uses text-embedding-3-small; external baselines retain their default embeddings. SHDocQA and MHDocQA use substring matching, and DetectiveQA uses letter exact matching. LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S use a gpt-4o-mini judge with majority-of-3 voting. MemoryCD uses ROUGE-1, ROUGE-L, BLEU-4, and BERTScore-F1. Agent backbones and evaluation protocols are specified in Section 3.3. Differences in accuracy or success rate are reported in percentage points.

Efficiency and uncertainty.

We report total ingestion wall-clock time, mean time to retrieve and answer a question, total answer tokens, and graph node and edge counts where available. Graph size measures index structure, not stored text length or total storage. For interactive agents, we report success, action steps, and training and test tokens, with mean and standard deviation over three runs. For LoCoMo, all comparisons below use the results in Table 1; M0, M1, and M2 are distinct system configurations, not repeated runs used to estimate variance.

3.2 User memory: recall, documents, and personalization

The hypergraph and AutoDream each improve conversational recall.

Figure 4 and Table 1, with Table 8 in the appendix, compare the M0, M1, and M2 configurations under the evaluation protocol described above and show a consistent ordering on both conversational benchmarks. On LoCoMo, graph retrieval raises overall accuracy from 85.7% for M0 to 88.4% for M1, and semantic AutoDream raises it to 91.4% for M2. On LongMemEval-S, the corresponding values are 58.8%, 70.0%, and 72.6%. The graph increment is thus 2.7 points on LoCoMo and 11.2 points on LongMemEval-S, while AutoDream adds 3.0 and 2.6 points, respectively. The larger graph increment on LongMemEval-S suggests that evidence organization can matter more when flat retrieval has difficulty recovering the relevant history. It does not establish which question types account for that gain, since a LongMemEval-S category breakdown is not available here.

Semantic consolidation can help temporal recall without rewriting events.

The LoCoMo breakdown is more informative than overall accuracy alone. Moving from M0 to M1 improves multi-hop accuracy by 5.7 points, compared with 1.0 point on temporal questions. Moving from M1 to M2 then improves every reported category, including 3.4 points on temporal questions. This pattern is consistent with the division of work in the method. N-ary frames connect related evidence, while identity consolidation gives retrieval a more coherent entry point into records that mention the same entity. Since semantic AutoDream preserves fact nodes and episodic occurrences, temporal evidence can become easier to reach without collapsing distinct events. This is an interpretation of the aggregate results; a direct audit of retrieved records and merged anchors would be needed to establish the mechanism for individual answers.

Figure 5 compares MIRIX-2.0 with all memory baselines on the five QA benchmarks. M2 exceeds HyperMem by 0.4 points overall on LoCoMo and by 14.3 points on LongMemEval-S. Its LoCoMo advantage is concentrated in temporal and multi-hop questions, with gains of 5.0 and 0.7 points, while HyperMem retains higher open-domain and single-hop scores. The evidence therefore supports stronger recovery of connected and time-grounded facts, rather than dominance on every form of recall. HyperMem’s 91.0% comes from our own run and is lower than the 92.7% it reports. Section B.1 describes how we ran HyperMem with its original settings.

Keeping source details improves document QA.

Table 8 in the appendix reports M1 on document QA. Its 83.0% on SHDocQA and 71.0% on MHDocQA exceed HyperMem by 31.0 and 22.0 points. Gains on both tasks are consistent with a design that retains source details as well as relational structure. Single-hop questions require the precise fact, while multi-hop questions also require connections between supporting records. In Sections 2.2 and 2.4, these requirements motivate source-faithful writers and retrieval of original rows alongside graph facts. The comparison measures the combined pipeline and does not isolate either feature.

DetectiveQA exposes a boundary of this advantage. M1 reaches 64.8%, below MemoryBank’s 67.6% and HyperMem’s 66.2%. Organizing explicit evidence does not by itself guarantee the inference needed to resolve a detective question. Without an error analysis, we cannot distinguish missed evidence from failures to reason over retrieved evidence. The document results also cannot establish an AutoDream benefit, because they evaluate M1 only.

Selective user memory supports personalized generation.

Table 2, and Table 9 in the appendix, move from answering factual questions to generating text for a particular user. Cross-domain evaluation is especially relevant because useful preferences must transfer from other product domains to Home_and_Kitchen. This tests a different role for semantic memory from recalling a named event. A useful record must preserve a user’s relevant preferences while remaining accessible when the new request has a different surface topic.

For cross-domain summarization, MIRIX-2.0 has the highest value on all four metrics. Its ROUGE-L is .1510, compared with .1430 for the strongest baseline on that metric, and its BLEU-4 is .0209, compared with .0162. In the single-domain setting it leads on ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-L and ties the highest BERTScore, while long-context input has higher BLEU-4. Review generation shows the highest reported scores for MIRIX-2.0 in both settings on all four metrics, although several margins are small. Together, these results suggest that selective user memory can preserve useful information for generation without requiring the full history as context. They do not measure factual consistency, preference satisfaction, or user approval directly, and the available configuration record does not support a MemoryCD-specific claim about graph or AutoDream gains.

3.3 Agent memory: held-out tasks and skills

Setup and transfer to held-out tasks.

We evaluate procedural memory on ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021) and WebShop (Yao et al., 2022), comparing an agent without memory with ReasoningBank (Ouyang et al., 2026), Agent Workflow Memory (AWM) (Wang et al., 2025e), and MIRIX-2.0. Within each comparison, methods share the actor prompt and backbone. ALFWorld uses GPT-6 Luna and GPT-5.6 Luna; WebShop uses GPT-6 Luna. Each memory method learns from the same training tasks, 39 for ALFWorld and 40 for WebShop. Memory is then frozen for evaluation on 134 held-out ALFWorld episodes with a 50-step cap and 140 WebShop instructions with a 15-step cap. Results are averaged over three independent runs. The separation between memory learning and evaluation tests reuse of acquired procedures on new tasks.

This setting exercises the procedural branch of AutoDream (Section 2.5). Sessions supply lessons to reuse and mistakes to avoid, and a curator turns those experiences into skills. Unlike semantic consolidation, which preserves the factual records and changes their index, procedural refinement changes the instructions available to the actor. The experiments evaluate the utility of that combined process; they do not separately ablate the outcome judge, experience distiller, or curator.

ALFWorld: useful procedures must generalize across action sequences.

Figure 6, and Table 10 in the appendix, show the highest mean overall success among the compared methods for MIRIX-2.0 with both backbones. With GPT-6 Luna it reaches 76.4%, compared with 69.4% without memory and 73.6% with AWM. With GPT-5.6 Luna it reaches 61.7%, compared with 54.2% and 58.0%, respectively. The gains over no memory are similar, at 7.0 and 7.5 points, but they are not uniform across task types (Figure 7). With GPT-6 Luna, Clean improves from 60.2% to 74.2% and Heat from 47.8% to 73.9%, while Pick, Look, and Pick Two remain below the no-memory scores. This suggests that procedures are most useful when they supply missing action structure; retrieving a routine can also interfere with a task the actor already handles well.

The step counts provide a complementary view. Successful episodes require 13.2 rather than 14.2 steps with GPT-6 Luna and 12.4 rather than 16.1 with GPT-5.6 Luna, relative to no memory. This is consistent with more direct action sequences, but the successful subsets differ across methods, so these are not paired measurements on identical solved tasks. The large success-rate standard deviations for MIRIX-2.0, 6.2 and 14.0 points, also limit the conclusion. It has the highest observed mean, but three runs do not establish a stable advantage over AWM.

WebShop: procedure quality matters more than memory availability.

Table 11 in the appendix reports 37.4% success for MIRIX-2.0, compared with 31.9% without memory, 25.7% with ReasoningBank, and 36.0% with AWM. ReasoningBank falls below no memory on both interactive benchmarks with GPT-6 Luna, showing that adding experience memory is not sufficient to improve an actor. In WebShop, MIRIX-2.0 leads the memory methods on Fashion and Beauty, ties AWM on Garden and Grocery, and trails AWM on Electronics. A plausible interpretation is that reusable constraint checks help some product searches, while other searches need more task-specific guidance. The category results do not directly identify which learned skills caused those differences.

MIRIX-2.0 uses 8.2 steps per episode and 6.3 per successful episode, fewer than the other memory methods but slightly more than no memory at 7.9 and 6.2. Thus, its benefit is a higher success rate with modest additional interaction, not a reduction in steps relative to every baseline.

MetaClaw-Bench: answer quality and completed artifacts are distinct.

Table 3 evaluates agent memory on Part I of MetaClaw-Bench (Xia et al., 2026b), which spans 30 days. Accuracy is the official mean per-question score, which combines binary file checks with partial credit on multiple-choice questions, and completion is the completion rate over the 224 file-check questions. With GPT-5.2, MIRIX-2.0 improves the official mean question score from 44.0% for MetaClaw Skills to 49.2%, and file-check completion from 17.1% to 27.7%. The larger completion gain, 10.6 points, suggests that reusable procedures can help produce the required artifacts as well as improve question scores. With Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, the score gain is smaller, from 51.8% to 52.7%, and completion is tied at 30.8%. The benefit therefore depends on the backbone and on what the metric measures. The GPT-5.2 baselines are reported values from the MetaClaw paper, so this comparison is not evidence from a fully controlled rerun. Unlike ALFWorld and WebShop, this table does not report variation across independent runs or a matched procedural-component ablation.

3.4 Efficiency: ingestion time, answer latency, and tokens

Graph construction moves work into ingestion.

Figure 8a and Table 12 in the appendix show the cost of organizing source records before queries arrive. Relative to M0, M1 increases ingestion time by 3.8 to 4.0 times across the three document tasks. M1 also has higher answer latency than M0 on each task, so graph retrieval is not intrinsically cheaper than flat retrieval. Its purpose is to improve access to structured evidence, with extraction and indexing paid in advance and additional evidence handling paid at query time.

Against HyperMem, M1 answers faster on all three document tasks (Figure 8b), at 5.45 versus 10.55 seconds on SHDocQA, 9.01 versus 10.65 on MHDocQA, and 7.24 versus 13.05 on DetectiveQA. It uses fewer answer tokens on SHDocQA and MHDocQA, but more on DetectiveQA, at 1.16M versus 0.35M. The DetectiveQA result shows that lower latency can coexist with higher token use and lower accuracy. Latency, token cost, and answer quality therefore need to be assessed separately.

The available timings characterize M1, not the full M2 system.

Figure 8b and Table 12 in the appendix show that M1 also has lower answer latency than HyperMem on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S, completing the five-benchmark latency comparison. Its conversational ingestion time is lower as well, unlike the document setting. These measurements are consistent with bounded graph access keeping answer latency low, but they do not isolate the effects of candidate caps, model calls, or execution conditions. M2 adds consolidation calls and can change subsequent retrieval behavior. Its total ingestion cost, answer cost, and graph reduction must be measured directly before attaching the M1 latency claims to the full system. Node and edge counts alone likewise do not quantify evidence retention or compression.

Fewer agent steps do not necessarily mean fewer tokens.

Table 4 separates the cost of learning a procedure from the cost of applying it, with the token accounting given in Section B.3. On WebShop, MIRIX-2.0 uses the fewest training and test tokens among the memory methods, 1.815M and 4.975M per run, while achieving the highest mean success. On ALFWorld, its 3.813M test tokens are the highest among the memory methods despite its lower mean step count. A retrieved procedure can reduce interaction steps while increasing the context processed at each step. Relative to no memory, test tokens rise on both benchmarks, so procedural memory should be judged by the resulting success and reuse, rather than assumed to save tokens automatically. The reported totals do not determine how many future tasks are needed to amortize memory learning, because no varying-horizon cost study is included.

3.5 What the experiments establish

The results support the three properties in different measure. Accuracy has the broadest support. The M0, M1, and M2 ordering holds on both conversational benchmarks, and MIRIX-2.0 leads the compared systems on four of the five QA benchmarks, two of them with AutoDream disabled. As procedural memory, it has the highest mean success among the compared memory methods on ALFWorld with both backbones and on WebShop, and the highest MetaClaw-Bench score with both backbones, while the no-memory comparisons show that retrieved experience can also hurt. Efficiency holds for answering more than for ingestion. With AutoDream disabled, MIRIX-2.0 answers faster than HyperMem on every timed benchmark, and on WebShop it uses the fewest training and test tokens among the memory methods. Graph construction, however, makes document ingestion 3.8 to 4.0 times slower than flat memory, and the ALFWorld test tokens of MIRIX-2.0 are the highest among the memory methods. Practicality rests on the design and on our protocol rather than on a deployment. One store serves both uses, no model is fine-tuned, and every graph fact returned to the answerer cites its source rows.

The tables evaluate complete configurations, so the component explanations in this section remain interpretations, and the limitations in Section 5 list the ablations that would test them. The tables also do not measure merge precision, source-detail retention, skill provenance coverage, or the contribution of the six-writer routing policy, and they do not report memory length or user-memory ingestion tokens, for which graph counts and answer tokens cannot substitute.

4 Related Work

Memory systems for LLM agents.

Memory systems for LLM agents keep past interactions outside the model and retrieve them when they become relevant (Huang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2025c; Wang et al., 2025a; Guo et al., 2026). Early designs rank or decay a memory stream (Park et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2024) or manage memory the way an operating system manages storage (Packer et al., 2023; Kang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). Later systems extract and update salient facts (Chhikara et al., 2025), link notes into an evolving network (Xu et al., 2025), compress what they store (Fang et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026a), or learn memory construction with reinforcement learning (Wang et al., 2025d; Yan et al., 2026). Graph memories organize content around entities and their relations (Bei et al., 2025; Rasmussen et al., 2025; Gutiérrez et al., 2024; Gutiérrez et al., 2025; Edge et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2026b), and hypergraph memories keep n-ary facts together (Luo et al., 2025a; Yue et al., 2026). Typed designs split memory by function, following cognitive accounts of episodic and semantic memory (Tulving, 1985; Pink et al., 2025). MIRIX (Wang and Chen, 2025) assigns six memory types to dedicated agents, and PersonaAgent (Zhang et al., 2026e) pairs episodic and semantic memory for personalization. Memory stored in model parameters or latent states (Wang et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025c; Behrouz et al., 2025) requires training and cannot be used with closed models. Evaluation has moved from recall over long conversations (Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025) to multi-session agentic tasks (Hu et al., 2026; He et al., 2026), evolving environments (Ji et al., 2026), lifelong personalization (Zhang et al., 2026d), memory audits (Ma et al., 2026b), and comparisons of memory substrates (Huang et al., 2026c). MIRIX-2.0 combines the typed and the graph directions. Complete typed records remain the system of record, a provenance hypergraph serves only as their index, and every graph fact cites its source records.

Multi-agent systems.

Multi-agent systems divide a task among LLM agents that take different roles (Guo et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025b), from role-playing and conversable agents (Li et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024) to software teams and groups of experts (Hong et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024). Agents can debate (Du et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2024; Huang and Caragea, 2026), optimize their workflow (Zhuge et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b), or communicate through latent representations (Yang et al., 2026). They also fail in new ways (Cemri et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026a), and one response keeps humans in the loop as collaborators (Zou et al., 2025a; Zou et al., 2025b; Wu et al., 2026a). Memory in these systems mostly serves the collaboration, through shared pools, graphs of team trajectories, and sharing across users under access control (Gao and Zhang, 2026; Zhang et al., 2025a; Rezazadeh et al., 2025). MIRIX-2.0 applies the multi-agent design to memory itself. A Meta Memory Manager routes each input to the agents of the six memory types, and each agent writes only the records of its own type.

Self-reflection and memory consolidation.

Self-reflection lets an agent improve from feedback on its own behavior without updating its weights (Shinn et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2023; Park et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025). Experience-driven methods turn such feedback into reusable knowledge, including insights (Zhao et al., 2024), executable skills (Wang et al., 2024a), workflows (Wang et al., 2025e), reasoning strategies (Ouyang et al., 2026), and evolving playbooks and case banks (Suzgun et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c; Fang et al., 2026b; Zhou et al., 2025). Skills can co-evolve with the policy (Xia et al., 2026a; Xia et al., 2026b), be verified and optimized as artifacts (Zhang et al., 2026b; Ma et al., 2026a), or form a hypergraph (Xu et al., 2026), and agents, their harnesses, and their memory architectures can improve themselves (Xia et al., 2026d; Xia et al., 2026c; Liu et al., 2026b; Gao et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2025). Consolidation can also run offline, before queries arrive or while the user is inactive (Lin et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2026a; Xia et al., 2026b; Ye et al., 2026). Rewriting memory carries risks. Consolidated memories can become faulty (Zhang et al., 2026a), and a defective skill can contaminate the skills distilled after it (Shang et al., 2026). AutoDream also consolidates outside the write path, but it limits what consolidation may change. On semantic memory it merges only anchors that denote the same entity and never rewrites stored records. On procedural memory it keeps a judged outcome, and each experience a skill edit cites, only after checking the quoted text.

5 Conclusion

We presented MIRIX-2.0, a multi-agent memory system that keeps complete typed records, indexes them with a provenance hypergraph under explicit budgets, and runs AutoDream outside the write path to merge duplicate anchors and refine skills. It leads the compared systems on four of the five QA benchmarks, two of them with AutoDream disabled, reaching 91.4% on LoCoMo and 72.6% on LongMemEval-S, and it has the highest value on all four metrics for cross-domain review summarization on MemoryCD. On LoCoMo, the hypergraph and AutoDream each add accuracy over flat memory. As procedural memory, its distilled skills lead the compared memory methods in mean success on ALFWorld and WebShop, and with GPT-5.2 they reach 49.2% on MetaClaw-Bench, against 44.0% reported for the MetaClaw skill library. With AutoDream disabled, MIRIX-2.0 answers each question in less time than HyperMem on all five timed benchmarks, and on WebShop its skills cost the fewest tokens among the memory methods. One store serves both uses, and the system runs with closed and open models without fine-tuning. The results suggest that a memory layer can be practical, accurate, and efficient at once when complete records remain the system of record, the graph is only a bounded index, and consolidation changes how evidence is connected rather than what evidence exists.

Limitations.

Our ablations add components in groups. They do not isolate n-ary frames, cited source rows, occurrence identities, answer-time verification, or the judge, distiller, and curator of procedural memory, so the explanations in Section 3 remain interpretations. The user-memory results come from single runs, partly scored by an LLM judge, the agent results average three runs with large spreads, and some baselines are values reported by their authors.

Ethics and Broader Impact Statement

MIRIX-2.0 lets assistants and task agents carry what users told them, and what the agents learned, from one session to the next. Every graph fact cites the records it was extracted from, so an answer can be traced to stored evidence. It is intended for assistants that users knowingly choose to use and should not be used to build profiles of people without their consent. A user-centric memory accumulates personal and possibly sensitive information. MIRIX-2.0 keeps sensitive verbatim values in a Knowledge Vault that the hypergraph does not index, but this does not replace consent and access control. A deployment should let users view, correct, and delete their memories, confine each memory to its user (Rezazadeh et al., 2025), and use model providers or local models that meet its privacy requirements, because stored content is sent to the model. Memory can also make mistakes persistent (Zhang et al., 2026a; Shang et al., 2026), and content injected into a conversation can be stored and later retrieved as if it were trusted. A wrong merge changes only the index, and a procedural edit keeps a citation only after its quote is checked, but in high-stakes settings learned skills and merged identities should still be reviewed by a person and stored memories audited periodically (Ma et al., 2026b). All experiments use publicly released benchmarks under their licenses. We collected no new data and ran no study with human participants. MemoryCD is built from public Amazon product reviews, and we use it as released without attempting to identify the reviewers.
