Appendix A Method details

This appendix collects the details of Section 2 that the main text summarizes or leaves out, in the order of its subsections. For each part it states the constants, schedules, scoring rules, and examples, explains why they are designed as they are, and names the step of Algorithm 1 they belong to.

A.1 Memory types, routing, and writing

The Meta Memory Manager is the first call of the write path (Algorithm 1, line 2). The router reads the input and selects the memory types it updates. Each selected writer then reads the current store Put−1P_{u}^{t-1} and produces a record that line 3 commits to the evidence plane before any graph work begins. Formally, each input xtx_{t} is mapped to a subset of six specialized writers,

𝒦t\displaystyle\mathcal{K}_{t} =Rθ​(xt),\displaystyle=R_{\theta}(x_{t}), (A.1)
mt(k)\displaystyle m_{t}^{(k)} =Wk(xt,Put−1),k∈𝒦t,\displaystyle=W_{k}(x_{t},P_{u}^{t-1}),\quad k\in\mathcal{K}_{t},

and each writer owns the schema and update operations of one memory type. Both steps of (A.1) are language-model calls, which is why the router and the writers carry the ⋆\star mark in Algorithm 1. Table 5 lists the six types.

The separation is functional. Only episodic and semantic memory are indexed by the hypergraph, because they hold the event and relational evidence that cross-memory traversal needs. The other types keep their direct, type-specific retrieval paths. Core memory holds the persistent state of the user and the agent, procedural memory holds the skills that Section 2.5 refines, resource memory holds documents and multimodal artifacts, and the knowledge vault holds sensitive verbatim values. Each of them is read through its own typed path rather than through the graph. In Algorithm 1, the test k∈{episodic,semantic}k\in\{\mathrm{episodic},\mathrm{semantic}\} is the only step of the write path that depends on whether a record is graph-indexed. In Figure 2, both user turns are routed to the episodic and semantic writers.

Source-faithful writing.

Before a record reaches the graph extractor, the writer prompts of our runs ask the episodic and semantic writers to keep complete lists, names, counts, titles, locations, and dates in the record’s details instead of replacing them with a topical gist. Episodic writers store the time an event happened rather than the time it was mentioned, and they store a planned event with its planned date.

Write ordering.

The write to the vector database commits before graph construction begins (line 3). Graph extraction is a fail-soft indexing hook, so a graph failure is logged but never rolls back a stored memory. The evidence plane is thus the durable system of record rather than a side effect of graph construction.

A.2 Anchor admission, canonicalization, and frame extraction

This part details lines 5 to 9 of Algorithm 1, which turn a committed episodic or semantic record into the anchors and frames of Section 2.3.

Anchor keys and admission.

The key κ⁡(n)\kappa(n) of an anchor name normalizes case, punctuation, articles and other function words, word order, and conservative singular and plural variants while keeping numbers. In the code it lowercases the name, replaces punctuation with spaces, drops a fixed list of eleven articles and function words, singularizes tokens of at least four letters, and sorts the remaining tokens, so that Mobile App and Mobile Apps share one key. The key is deliberately conservative. Numbers and dates are preserved, so 10 Gallons and 20 Gallons stay distinct, and only plural endings are normalized, so Training and Trains stay apart. A single admission gate rejects generic filing terms, such as advice, details, information, plan, and tips, and dialogue-role pseudo-entities such as user and assistant, and it keeps at most 16 anchors for an episodic record and 18 for a semantic one. The caps bound the anchor space of a user, and they are sized for the arguments of an assertion rather than for a bag of keywords, so that one frame with seven arguments does not exhaust them. The gate is the Admit call of Algorithm 1, and because it runs on the canonical key, one entry such as user also blocks User, Users, and the user.

Registry-guided canonicalization.

For every extracted entity, approximate nearest-neighbor search retrieves up to four existing anchors of the user whose cosine similarity is at least 0.720.72, and one language-model call per record makes a conservative same-entity decision for all of its entities. The vector index scores a pair by (1+cos)/2(1+\cos)/2, so the thresholds in the code are 0.86 here and 0.93 for AutoDream (Section A.5). The call is instructed not to merge different quantities, different days or months, different form or model codes, or related but distinct concepts. Canonicalization runs before the admission gate, which is the order Admit​(Canon⋆​(Φ))\textsc{Admit}(\textsc{Canon}^{\star}(\Phi)) of Algorithm 1, so the gate judges canonical names rather than surface forms. The candidates come from the anchors the user already has, which is what keeps naming consistent as the graph grows and why we call the step registry-guided.

Frames, literals, and repair.

The extractor behind (5) is instructed to keep dates, prices, counts, durations, and measurements as literals on the frame rather than as anchors, so that values such as 7, $420, or three months stay attached to the assertion they qualify. A frame is materialized only if its arguments resolve to at least two distinct anchors of the user, which is the test |Af|≥2|A_{f}|\geq 2 of Algorithm 1. When a deterministic audit finds that the extraction misses high-signal source details, such as quoted phrases, numbers, or concrete visual content, one bounded repair call may add frames that the source supports. The repair cannot remove anything the primary extraction produced. The audit compares the words of the rendered frames with the source text. It lists the quoted phrases and the numbers of the source that the frames do not cover, it treats a source with visual content as uncovered when the frames cover less than 45 percent of its content words, and it sends at most twelve missing items to the repair call. A missing date alone does not trigger a repair, because session dates recur in many records and are already preserved by provenance. A missing date is added to a call that a missing quote, number, or visual detail already requires. Repair is the Repair⋆\textsc{Repair}^{\star} call of line 5, and the frames it adds pass through the same canonicalization, admission, and identity rules as the primary ones.

A.3 Retrieval budgets, lanes, scores, and fusion

This part details the Read procedure of Algorithm 1, whose steps Section 2.4 introduces.

Operator budgets.

The planner (9) fixes two row budgets for every query, and Table 6 lists them by operator. The budgets grow with the operator, because counting and set construction need broader evidence than a single-value lookup. A single-value question needs the one row that holds the value, so its cited-row budget is the smallest, whereas a count has to see many members of the set it counts. The evidence a question inspects is therefore bounded by its operator and not by the length of the history.

Anchor entry.

Beyond the fifteen anchors that vector recall returns, a relation query adds up to sixteen anchors that the question names exactly before the union is scored by (10). Person hubs receive a larger penalty unless a relation query names them explicitly. Only the exactly named anchors carry degree and predicate information, so the hub and predicate terms act on them alone. The two entry routes serve different questions. Vector recall finds the anchors whose names paraphrase the question, and exact lookup finds the anchors that a relation question names, so that the relation lane can start from the named participants rather than from their nearest paraphrases.

Two evidence lanes.

The lanes follow three rules beyond those of Section 2.4. In the base-recall lane, same-chunk support and immediate temporal neighbors are recomputed from the provenance stored in the vector database instead of being duplicated as graph bookkeeping edges. In the relation-citation lane, predicate filtering runs inside Neo4j before the cap of 240 frames, and when the question names a concrete object, only frames that contain it are kept. The base lane is the Rows​(Aq)\textsc{Rows}(A_{q}) term and the relation lane the Adj​(Aq,𝒫q)\textsc{Adj}(A_{q},\mathcal{P}_{q}) term of Algorithm 1. Recomputing same-chunk and temporal neighbors from provenance keeps the graph free of edges that only restate what the evidence plane already records. Filtering by predicate inside the database before the cap means that an explicitly named hub with hundreds of incident frames does not trigger a full traversal, and the frames that survive the cap are selected by a deterministic order on the frame identifier, so which frames pass does not depend on the traversal order of the database.

Fact scoring.

Two details of (11) complete Section 2.4. When a frame has no extracted event time, the state term sstates_{\mathrm{state}} falls back at half weight to the time of the source record, so the frame can still compete on time. For intersection questions, a hard shared-object group is preserved before these soft refinements, so recency cannot replace evidence that satisfies only one side of the intersection. The role term reads the typed roles of a frame, and the state term reads the status literal that marks an event as planned or completed (Section 2.3), which is how planned events are penalized in count, list-union, and temporal questions.

Citation-balanced fusion.

Rows in each lane are reranked with a shallow vector-rank prior and the lexical coverage of the query. Fusion runs separately for episodic and semantic rows within the row limit of a request. Near-duplicate episodic paraphrases are collapsed only when they share a calendar date, so the same wording on two different dates stays separate. Cited rows are filled first because a graph fact without the row that supports it would leave the answer unverifiable, and the date condition on paraphrase collapse is the retrieval-side counterpart of the occurrence identity (7), which keeps undated repetitions apart at write time.

A.4 Answer-time verification

The Answer procedure of Algorithm 1 belongs to the evaluation harness rather than to the memory server, and the rule-based check of Section 2.4 never inspects a reference answer. The check fires when it finds explicit uncertainty, a count without a number or one that disagrees with a listed count, a temporal answer without a time, an answer number or month that is absent from the evidence ledger and the question, ledger evidence with an incompatible role, or a planned event in a count question. It also fires on every intersection question. The extra search uses a query derived from Π⁡(q)\Pi(q), or the question itself for a relation query. Most triggers mark a way in which a draft falls short of the evidence it was given or disagrees with it. A number or month that appears in neither the ledger nor the question was not retrieved, a count that disagrees with a listed count contradicts the evidence, and a planned event in a count question would count something that has not happened. Intersection questions always trigger the check because they need evidence for both sides, and a first retrieval that satisfies one side can look complete. The rewrite is line 19 of Algorithm 1, so the procedure adds at most one search and one model call to a question.

A.5 AutoDream schedule, candidates, and procedural refinement

This part details the SemanticDream and ProceduralDream procedures of Algorithm 1 (lines 22 to 29) and expands Section 2.5.

Invocation protocol.

Semantic AutoDream is an explicit service call that never schedules itself. In our protocol, the ingestion driver invokes AutoDream after every five chunks and once after the final chunk. The chunk identifiers of each call resolve to the newly written semantic rows, which define the frontier Δu\Delta_{u} of (12), and the eligible anchors backed by those rows are the sources 𝒜Δ\mathcal{A}_{\Delta} of (13). An intermediate call therefore examines only the anchors whose semantic rows the batch just wrote, and the final call also considers the eligible anchors that no earlier call used as a source.

Candidate generation.

The identity-stable types 𝒯safe\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{safe}} of Section 2.5 are person, organization, location, object, and concept. Anchors of the types event, date, content, method, and other are excluded deliberately, because merging two of them can collapse distinct occurrences or temporal context even when their names are close in embedding space. Both endpoints of a candidate pair must be backed by semantic rows and share the same eligible type, and the cosine threshold 0.860.86 of (13) is the index score 0.930.93 under the (1+cos)/2(1+\cos)/2 scale of Section A.2.

Bounded schedule.

An intermediate Dream verifies at most 80 unseen pairs from the current semantic delta. The final Dream considers the delta together with eligible anchors that have never served as a Dream source, and it verifies at most 120 pairs. If that round merges anything, one repair round examines only the touched representatives and verifies at most 60 more pairs. Explicit negative decisions are cached by anchor type, so later cycles do not pay again to reconsider the same pair. The cache key hashes the case-folded pair in sorted order together with the type, so the order in which a pair is encountered does not matter. Only explicit rejections are cached. A pair that a round did not reach within its cap is not recorded as rejected, so it becomes a candidate again whenever one of its anchors is in a later frontier. The intermediate rounds keep the graph consolidated while ingestion proceeds, and the final round sweeps up anchors that earlier rounds never used as a source. In Algorithm 1, the cache is the set 𝒩\mathcal{N} that line 22 subtracts from the candidate pairs, and the per-round caps bound the number of Same⋆\textsc{Same}^{\star} calls the loop makes.

Procedural refinement.

Two rules of the procedural path complete Section 2.5. The distiller judges the outcome of each pending session from quotes in its transcript, and an outcome whose quotes do not occur in the transcript is downgraded to unclear rather than trusted. Besides creating, editing, or deleting a skill, the curator can mark an experience as already covered, not worth a skill, or deferred, so it can decline an experience without changing the store. The quote check on outcomes and the quote check on citations are the procedural counterpart of the provenance that the hypergraph keeps for facts. They keep the skill library traceable although both Distill⋆\textsc{Distill}^{\star} and Curate⋆\textsc{Curate}^{\star} in Algorithm 1 are language-model calls.

A.6 Invariants, learned decisions, and complexity

Hard invariants.

Four properties hold regardless of model behavior.

  1. 1.

    Every returned graph fact exposes the identifiers of its source memories.

  2. 2.

    Undated episodic occurrences from different memory rows receive different frame identities.

  3. 3.

    Retrieval and Dream both run under explicit candidate and output caps.

  4. 4.

    A failed graph write cannot destroy a committed memory, and a graph read that raises an error falls back to direct evidence retrieval.

Together with Equation 12, the first and fourth invariants give the source fidelity required in Section 2.1, the third gives bounded access, and the second gives temporal identity.

Learned and deterministic decisions.

Language models route inputs, write typed memories, extract frames, repair missing source details, judge semantic identity, and distill and curate procedural experience. Together with answer generation, these are the calls marked ⋆\star in Algorithm 1. Deterministic code owns the safety-critical boundaries, namely admissible anchor names, candidate allowlists, frame identities, the representation of events and their status, provenance attachment, query operators, lane budgets, merge algebra, and mutation order. An LLM may propose that two anchors are identical, for instance, but it cannot name an anchor outside the retrieved candidate set or delete evidence directly.

Complexity.

Let dd be the number of admitted anchors in one memory, hh the number of frames extracted from it, KAK_{A} the anchor-retrieval cap, and KFK_{F} the adjacent-frame cap. Ignoring model inference and indexed database lookups, writing a memory into the graph costs O⁡(d+h)O(d+h). Post-retrieval ranking and fusion cost O⁡(KA+KF+KM)O(K_{A}+K_{F}+K_{M}), where KMK_{M} is the operator-dependent cited-row budget, and the system never materializes an unbounded evidence set from the vector database. For a Dream frontier of size |Δu||\Delta_{u}|, nearest-neighbor generation costs O⁡(|Δu|​log⁡|𝒜u|)O(|\Delta_{u}|\log|\mathcal{A}_{u}|) under the vector index, and LLM verification is capped at 80 pairs per intermediate cycle and 180 pairs across the two possible final rounds. The constants behind these symbols are the ones of this appendix. The admission gate bounds dd by 16 for an episodic record and 18 for a semantic one (Section A.2), KAK_{A} is the fifteen anchors kept after scoring, KFK_{F} is the cap of 240 frames, and KMK_{M} is BqRB_{q}^{R}, at most 12 (Section A.3). The 180 final pairs are the 120 of the final round plus the 60 of its repair round (Section A.5).

A.7 Implementation and an example hypergraph

Evidence rows are stored in a vector database and the hypergraph in Neo4j. Figure 9 shows part of the hypergraph that MIRIX-2.0 builds for LoCoMo conversation conv-26, in which Caroline and Melanie talk from May to October 2023. The full graph has 792 anchors, 1,379 frames, and 3,303 role edges. The figure keeps the 32 anchors that appear in the most frames, leaving out generic duplicates such as Family and kids, together with the 448 frames that join at least two of them.

The two speakers are the largest hubs, with 650 and 529 frames. Topics that one speaker raises gather on that speaker’s side, such as the pride parade and Becoming Nicole for Caroline and pottery and her family for Melanie. The 94 frames that join only the two speakers lie between the hubs and are drawn in gray, and painting and art are reached from both sides. Each frame also keeps role labels, literals such as dates, and citations to its source records, which the figure leaves out. Through these frames one anchor gathers evidence across sessions. Self-Acceptance appears in 13 frames from 10 sessions, which link it to the LGBTQ support group, the pride parade, Becoming Nicole, and Caroline’s painting Embracing Identity.

We built this graph with graph indexing and AutoDream enabled, using Claude Haiku 5.5 for extraction and Cohere Embed v4 for embeddings instead of the models described in Section 3.1.

Appendix B Additional results

This appendix gives the full tables behind Figures 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8. Accuracy and success rates are percentages, and differences are in points.

B.1 User memory

Table 8 lists the LongMemEval-S accuracy of every system, judged like LoCoMo by gpt-4o-mini with majority-of-3 voting. It reports M0, M1, and M2, so it complements the LoCoMo ablation of Table 1. Table 8 gives the results on the three document QA tasks of MemoryAgentBench. SHDocQA and MHDocQA ask single-hop and multi-hop questions about long documents and use substring matching on 100 questions each, and DetectiveQA uses letter exact matching on 71 questions. The document QA runs use M1, with AutoDream disabled by experimental choice.

We ran HyperMem ourselves with its original settings unchanged, and all HyperMem results in this paper come from these runs. On LoCoMo, our run reaches 91.0%, below the 92.7% reported by Yue et al. [2026].

On LongMemEval-S the graph increment of 11.2 points accounts for most of the 14.3-point margin over HyperMem. The flat configuration M0 reaches 58.8%, close to HyperMem at 58.3% and mem0 at 56.3%, while M1 reaches 70.0% and M2 72.6%, 14.3 points above HyperMem. On SHDocQA and MHDocQA, HyperMem is the strongest baseline, and M1 leads it by 31.0 and 22.0 points. DetectiveQA is the exception. MemoryBank leads with 67.6%, followed by HyperMem with 66.2% and M1 with 64.8%. A-Mem varies the most across the three document tasks, from 14.0% on SHDocQA to 62.0% on DetectiveQA.

Table 9 completes the MemoryCD results of Table 2 with review generation for the same 100 users in the Home_and_Kitchen domain. In both MemoryCD tables, cross-domain memory comes from the other three Amazon domains, and single-domain memory and testing use the same domain, so the cross-domain setting asks whether preferences stored for other products carry over to a new domain. R-1, R-L, B-4, and BERT denote ROUGE-1, ROUGE-L, BLEU-4, and BERTScore-F1, higher is better, and bold marks column maxima, including ties.

MIRIX-2.0 has the highest value in every column of both settings, but the margins are small. In the cross-domain setting its ROUGE-L of .1491 is .0057 above the next best, .1434 for Long-context and A-Mem, and its BLEU-4 of .0108 is .0014 above A-Mem. BERTScore spans at most .006 across all systems in either setting. In the single-domain setting the margins shrink further, for example .2868 against .2865 for Long-context on ROUGE-1.

B.2 Agent memory

Table 10 breaks down the ALFWorld success rates of Figure 6 by task type for both backbones, with the number of held-out episodes of each type in parentheses, 134 in total. All is the overall success rate, given as the mean and the sample standard deviation over three runs. Average steps are taken over all episodes, with a cap of 50 steps, and over successful episodes only, and lower is better. For each model, bold marks the best of the three memory methods. Figure 7 plots the GPT-6 Luna rows.

With GPT-6 Luna, MIRIX-2.0 is the best of the three memory methods on four of the six task types, Pick, Look, Clean, and Pick Two, and AWM is ahead on Heat and Cool. Against no memory, Clean gains 14.0 points, Heat 26.1, and Cool 4.7, while Pick, Look, and Pick Two lose 4.1, 1.9, and 3.9 points. With GPT-5.6 Luna, MIRIX-2.0 leads the memory methods on Look, Clean, and Cool and ties AWM on Heat at 63.8%, while ReasoningBank is ahead on Pick and AWM on Pick Two. With both backbones MIRIX-2.0 takes the fewest steps, 21.9 and 26.8 over all episodes and 13.2 and 12.4 over successful ones, but its overall standard deviation of 14.0 points with GPT-5.6 Luna is the largest in the table.

Table 11 gives the same breakdown for WebShop with GPT-6 Luna over the five product categories of the 140 test instructions, with a cap of 15 steps. A WebShop episode succeeds when its reward is 1, and bold again marks the best of the three memory methods.

MIRIX-2.0 has the highest overall success, 37.4% against 36.0% for AWM and 31.9% without memory, and the smallest spread among the memory methods, 2.1 points. Its margins over AWM are 4.5 points on Fashion and 8.0 on Beauty. It matches AWM on Garden and Grocery, at 27.1% and 38.1%, and trails it by 3.4 points on Electronics. ReasoningBank falls below no memory overall, as it does on ALFWorld with both backbones, and on four of the five categories. All three memory methods take more steps over all episodes than no memory, 8.2 to 10.2 against 7.9, and MIRIX-2.0 takes the fewest of the three.

B.3 Costs

Table 12 gives the measurements behind Figure 8. Ingest is the total wall-clock time in seconds, and Ans./q is the mean time to retrieve and answer one question. Answer tokens sum input and output over all questions, where K and M denote thousands and millions. Graph size counts Neo4j nodes and edges and excludes the evidence store. M0 builds no graph, and for HyperMem the column names its index type instead of a size. None of these measurements includes AutoDream, so they characterize M1 and not the full M2 system.

Table 12 shows where graph construction costs time. On the three document tasks, M1 ingests 3.8 to 4.0 times more slowly than M0 and 3.4 to 5.0 times more slowly than HyperMem. On the conversational benchmarks the order reverses, and M1 needs 21,416 s for LoCoMo against 69,467 s for HyperMem and 70,626 s for LongMemEval-S against 170,224 s. Answering is faster for M1 than for HyperMem on all five benchmarks, by between 0.63 s per question on LongMemEval-S and 5.81 s on DetectiveQA, although M0 answers the document questions faster still. M1 uses fewer answer tokens than HyperMem on four benchmarks and more on DetectiveQA, 1.16M against 0.35M. Its graphs range from 23,820 nodes and 32,394 edges for LoCoMo to 181,131 nodes and 205,428 edges for LongMemEval-S.

For Table 4, training covers actor interactions and memory learning, and testing covers actor interactions and memory retrieval on all test tasks, including unsuccessful ones. Counts include LLM input and output tokens, with reasoning tokens in the output and cached tokens in the input, and exclude embedding tokens. No memory skips training.
